title: What makes an animal an animal
description: Animals are many-celled organisms whose cells lack cell walls; they eat other living or dead things, and most can move at some stage of life. Sponges pass the test.

facts.text: Animals are multicellular eukaryotes, and unlike plants and fungi, their cells have no cell walls.
All animals need a source of food: they are heterotrophs, eating other living or dead organisms rather than making their own food.
Most animals can move, at least during some stage of life.
Sponges, which lack muscle tissue, were long considered plants; only after their small movements were noticed in 1765 did their animal nature slowly come to be recognized.
Sponge larvae can swim, but adult sponges do not move from place to place: they spend their lives attached to a surface.
A sponge feeds by filtering water through its porous body; tiny hairlike flagella create currents that bring in bacteria to eat, along with oxygen.

title: The main groups of animals
description: The animal kingdom includes five familiar groups (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish) and a huge crowd of animals without backbones, from insects and crabs to snails, worms, jellyfish, sea stars and sponges.

facts.text: Vertebrates are grouped as fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
Invertebrates include sea stars, sea urchins, earthworms, sponges, jellyfish, lobsters, crabs, insects, spiders, snails, clams and squid.

title: How many animal species are named
description: About 1.5 million animal species have been described, according to IUCN's 2025 table; about 1 million of them are insects. The figure is a snapshot, not an exact count.

facts.text: The IUCN Red List's 2025 table estimates about 1.55 million described animal species (roughly 1.5 million), including about 1 million insects; IUCN cautions the figures are not always up to date.

title: How many species may exist
description: A 2011 study by Camilo Mora and colleagues used patterns in how species sit inside better-known higher groups to estimate about 8.7 million eukaryote species, about 7.8 million of them animals; most are still undescribed.

facts.text: In 2011, Camilo Mora and colleagues estimated about 8.7 million species of eukaryotes on Earth, give or take 1.3 million, of which about 7.77 million (about 7.8 million) are animals.
Mora and colleagues found a steady numerical relationship between counts of the better-known higher groups in classification and the number of species, and used it to predict species numbers.

By the 2011 Mora estimate, about 86 percent of species on land and 91 percent in the ocean are still undescribed, and describing them all the traditional way could take up to 1,200 years and more than 300,000 taxonomists.

title: Vertebrates have a backbone
description: A vertebrate has a backbone, a column of vertebrae that partly encloses the central nervous system. The five vertebrate groups are fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.

facts.text: Vertebrates have a backbone (vertebral column), made of vertebrae, which partly encloses the central nervous system, including the spinal cord.

title: Most animals are invertebrates
description: Invertebrates, animals without a backbone, are about 95 percent of described animal species; many wear a hard outer skeleton instead.

facts.text: In the IUCN Red List's 2025 table, about 76,000 of roughly 1.55 million described animal species are vertebrates: roughly 1 in 20, leaving about 95 percent invertebrates.
An invertebrate is any animal without a backbone; more than 90 percent of all living animal species are invertebrates.
Many invertebrates, including most mollusks, crustaceans and insects, have a hard outer skeleton that protects the body and gives muscles something to attach to.

title: Two-part scientific names
description: Carl Linnaeus gave each species a two-part scientific name, genus then species, replacing long descriptive phrases; the system is used internationally, so one name points to one species. Zoological names start from 1758.

facts.text: Carl Linnaeus replaced long descriptive phrase names with two-part names, the genus followed by the species; he named humans Homo sapiens, and his system is internationally accepted among biologists.

The American robin (Turdus migratorius, about 25 cm long) and the European robin (Erithacus rubecula, about 14 cm long) are different birds; colonists named the American one robin because its breast colour resembled the European robin's.
The 10th edition of Linnaeus's Systema Naturae (1758) is the starting point of zoological nomenclature, as Species Plantarum (1753) is for plant names.

title: Ranks of classification
description: Species sit inside ever-larger groups: today's ranks run domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. Close relatives share a genus, like the big cats of Panthera.

facts.text: Linnaeus sorted living things into ranks including kingdom, class, order, genus and species; biologists added more ranks later.
The main ranks of classification today, from broadest to most specific, are domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species.
Lions, tigers, leopards and jaguars all belong to the genus Panthera: the leopard is Panthera pardus and the tiger Panthera tigris.

title: Endotherms and ectotherms
description: Endotherms (mainly mammals and birds) make most of their body heat inside and hold a steady temperature; ectotherms (fish, amphibians, reptiles, invertebrates) absorb it from their surroundings. "Cold-blooded" is misleading: a lizard can be warmer than some mammals.

facts.text: The terms warm-blooded and cold-blooded are imprecise and misleading: some cold-blooded lizards have higher normal body temperatures than some mammals.
Endothermy and ectothermy describe whether most of an animal's heat is generated by internal processes (endo-, inside) or absorbed from the environment (ecto-, outside).
Birds and mammals keep a relatively constant internal temperature whatever the weather: about 37 °C for mammals and about 40 °C for birds.
Fishes, amphibians, reptiles and invertebrates are cold-blooded (ectotherms): their body temperature varies with their surroundings, though they can control it somewhat by behavior such as basking.
Reptiles absorb heat by basking in the sun or lying on warm surfaces, and they move between sun and shade or change body position to control how much heat they gain or lose.

title: The food cost of making your own heat
description: Keeping a steady inside temperature costs energy: reptiles, with a low metabolic rate, need less food than endotherms of the same size and can go long periods without eating.

facts.text: Because reptiles do not keep a constant internal temperature, they have a low metabolic rate, need less food than warm-blooded animals of similar size, and can survive long periods without eating.

title: Herbivores, carnivores and omnivores
description: Herbivores eat mainly plants, carnivores mostly meat, and omnivores regularly eat both; teeth often reveal which.

facts.text: A herbivore feeds mostly on plants; herbivores range from aphids to elephants, and many herbivorous mammals have wide molars that grind leaves and grasses.
A carnivore eats mostly meat; carnivorous mammals have strong jaws and long, sharp teeth to grab and rip apart prey, and all cats, from house cats to tigers, must eat meat.

An omnivore regularly eats both plants and animals, as bears, raccoons and humans do (bears eat berries, mushrooms and animals such as salmon); a raccoon has sharp front teeth for ripping apart mice and large molars for chewing plants, and omnivores can switch foods if one runs out.

title: A diet label is not a family name
description: The giant panda belongs to the order Carnivora and kept a carnivore-like gut, yet it eats mostly bamboo: diet and classification answer different questions.

facts.text: The giant panda is a mammal in the order Carnivora and the bear family, with a digestive system more like a carnivore's, yet bamboo makes up most of its diet.
A giant panda cannot digest cellulose, the main material of bamboo, so it eats 70 to 100 pounds of bamboo a day and spends up to 16 hours a day eating.

title: Food chains and webs
description: A food chain runs from producers, which make their own food, through primary, secondary and tertiary consumers to apex predators, with decomposers recycling the dead; overlapping chains form a food web.

facts.text: Producers (autotrophs) make their own food and form the first level of every food chain; nearly all do it by photosynthesis, from sunlight, carbon dioxide and water.
Primary consumers (herbivores) eat producers, secondary consumers eat the herbivores, tertiary consumers eat the secondary consumers, and apex predators sit at the top.
Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria complete the food chain, turning dead plants and other organic wastes into nutrient-rich soil.
In one ocean food chain, single-celled phytoplankton feed tiny shrimp called krill, and krill are the main food of the blue whale.
All the interconnected and overlapping food chains in an ecosystem make up a food web.

title: The 10 percent rule
description: On average only about 10 percent of the energy at one food-chain level passes to the next; the rest is lost as waste, heat and uneaten dead, which is why most ecosystems have at most five levels.

facts.text: On average only about 10 percent of the energy at one trophic level passes to the next, so of 1,000 units of energy in producers, about 100 reach primary consumers and about 10 reach secondary consumers.

Energy is lost at each step because some food cannot be digested and is excreted, much escapes as heat during respiration, and some organisms die without being eaten; so most ecosystems support at most five trophic levels.

title: What an ecosystem is
description: An ecosystem is a place where living things and nonliving parts such as rocks, temperature and humidity work together; it can be as small as a tide pool, and every part depends on the others.

facts.text: An ecosystem is a geographic area where plants, animals and other organisms, along with weather and landscape, work together; it has living (biotic) parts and nonliving (abiotic) parts such as rocks, temperature and humidity.
Ecosystems come in many sizes: a tide pool is a complete, tiny ecosystem, and every part of an ecosystem depends on every other part, directly or indirectly.

title: Keystone species
description: A keystone species holds its ecosystem together, like the wedge stone at the top of an arch. Robert Paine showed it by removing sea stars from a Washington shore: mussels took over and variety collapsed.

facts.text: In the 1960s, ecologist Robert Paine pried carnivorous ochre sea stars, which eat mussels, off the rocks of Mukkaw Bay, Washington, with a crowbar and threw them into the sea as an experiment.

Within two years of removing the sea stars, California mussels took over rock that had supported anemones, sponges, barnacles, chitons, limpets and seaweeds, and diversity fell sharply; where the sea stars remained, the varied community persisted.
Paine coined the term keystone species for an organism that helps hold its ecosystem together; a keystone is the wedge-shaped stone at the top of an arch that keeps it from collapsing.

title: The largest animal ever
description: The blue whale, a living mammal, is the largest animal known to have lived: up to about 33 meters and more than 150 metric tons, feeding almost only on tiny krill.

facts.text: According to NOAA, the blue whale, a mammal, is the largest animal known to have lived on Earth.
In the Antarctic, blue whales can reach up to about 110 feet (about 33 meters) long and weigh more than 330,000 pounds (about 150 metric tons).
Blue whales feed almost exclusively on krill, and the biggest may eat up to 6 tons of krill a day.

title: The smallest animal record holders
description: The smallest known vertebrate is the Brazilian flea toad (males about 7.1 mm, 2024 study), just below Paedophryne amauensis (7.7 mm); the smallest known adult insects are male fairyfly wasps, as small as 0.139 mm.

facts.text: A February 2024 study in Zoologica Scripta found male Brazilian flea toads (Brachycephalus pulex) average 7.1 mm long, making them the smallest known vertebrate.
The previous smallest-vertebrate record holder was Paedophryne amauensis, a frog from Papua New Guinea whose males average about 7.7 mm.
Males of the fairyfly wasp Dicopomorpha echmepterygis, described in 1997, are the smallest known adult insects: blind, wingless and as small as 0.139 mm, smaller than a single-celled paramecium.
Derived: a 110-foot (about 33,500 mm) blue whale is more than 200,000 times longer than a 0.139 mm male fairyfly.

title: Sorting animals, and diets that change with age
description: Backbone, heat source and diet sort most animals, but some answers change with age: gray tree frog tadpoles eat algae and debris, while adults eat insects.

facts.text: Gray tree frog tadpoles eat algae and organic debris in the water, while adult gray tree frogs mainly prey on insects and their larvae.
